content_title: Measles resurges worldwide despite shrinking viral genetic diversity
content: As measles cases rebound and rubella remains difficult to track, a 25-year global review examines how changing viral genetics and gaps in disease surveillance complicate efforts to eliminate both infections. Review: Global Update on Measles and Rubella Molecular Epidemiology: 2000–2025 . Image Credit: Yau Ming Low / Shutterstock In a recent review of global surveillance data published in the journal Vaccines , researchers investigated the molecular epidemiology of measles and rubella ( MR ) viruses worldwide between 2000 and 2025, examining sequence submissions and the distribution of viral genotypes. An international team of researchers from the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), World Health Organization (WHO) headquarters and regional offices, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), and the Pasteur Institute of Tunis at University Tunis El Manar conducted the review, spanning institutions across nine countries. Measles virus ( MeV ) sequence submissions relative to reported cases have returned to pre-pandemic levels across all regions, but only two of the 24 historically recognized measles genotypes have been reported since 2021. The pandemic's impact on rubella surveillance remains difficult to determine, partly because few rubella virus ( RuV ) sequences are submitted to global surveillance databases. The review also outlines challenges facing the World Health Organization's ( WHO ) Global Measles and Rubella Laboratory Network ( GMRLN ) and stresses the need for continued member-state participation to strengthen molecular surveillance. Measles and rubella elimination remains a global public health priority. The WHO coordinates surveillance through GMRLN, which combines epidemiological reports and molecular data to track circulating strains and transmission. Member states contribute case reports and viral sequences to monitor genetic diversity, investigate outbreaks, and identify gaps in surveillance and vaccination. Global measles and rubella surveillance The review draws on global data from the Measles virus Nucleotide Surveillance ( MeaNS2 ) and Rubella virus Nucleotide Surveillance ( RubeNS2 ) databases through 2025. Most sequences are generated using reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction ( RT-PCR ) and Sanger sequencing. Only WHO GMRLN-accredited laboratories that pass annual laboratory proficiency tests can submit data. Member states must submit representative sequences covering 80% or more of transmission chains no later than eight weeks after sample receipt. MeV molecular surveillance relies mainly on the N-450 target, a 450-nucleotide segment located near the end of the nucleocapsid ( N ) gene. For RuV genotyping, laboratories examine a 739-nucleotide segment of the envelope glycoprotein 1 ( E1 ) gene, designated E-739 (739-bp window). The WHO compiles annual MR case figures using the Joint Reporting Form ( JRF ), developed jointly with UNICEF. MeV genotypes are classified according to sequence similarities in the hemagglutinin ( H ) and nucleoprotein (N) genes. Measles cases rebound after the pandemic A total of 411,913 measles cases were reported worldwide during 2025, returning to levels comparable to those before the pandemic. Reported cases are estimated to account for only around 5% of actual measles cases globally. Missed childhood vaccinations and resulting immunity gaps likely drove the resurgence. The extent to which pandemic-era declines reflected reduced transmission or disrupted surveillance remains unclear. Number of reported measles virus cases and sequence submissions to MeaNS2, stratified by WHO region. Reported case numbers were obtained from the WHO/UNICEF Joint Reporting Form (JRF), while sequence counts represent MeV sequences submitted by WHO GMRLN-accredited laboratories to MeaNS2. Transparency of grey bars indicates y-scale in that area of the plot and orders of magnitude between points. The European Region ( EUR ) recorded over 150,000 cases in 2024, its highest total since 1997, followed by a 75% decline in 2025. Cases rose from 2024 in the Region of the Americas ( AMR ), following previous regional measles elimination, while the African Region ( AFR ) and South-East Asia Region ( SEAR ) saw declines after their 2023 surges. Sequencing coverage was highest in the AMR, with a median annual ratio of submitted sequences to reported cases of 20% between 2000 and 2025, compared with 4% in the EUR and less than 1% in the other four WHO regions. Incomplete case reporting inflated AMR estimates, while representative outbreak sampling partly explains lower sequencing-to-case ratios in high-incidence regions. The EUR and Western Pacific Region ( WPR ) together contributed approximately 70% of sequences in MeaNS2. Annual distribution of MeV genotype B3 and D8 sequences submitted to MeaNS2, stratified by WHO region. Measles genetic diversity continues to decline The two remaining reported measles genotypes are B3 and D8. This reduction in genetic diversity is consistent with vaccination efforts limiting opportunities for viral transmission but makes distinguishing transmission chains through routine genotyping more difficult. D8 has been the most frequently reported genotype globally since 2018, except in 2021, and accounted for nearly all genetically characterized cases during the AMR resurgence in 2025. B3 was more common in the Eastern Mediterranean Region ( EMR ), while both genotypes were reported at comparable frequencies in the AFR and WPR. Europe also reported more B3 than D8 sequences in 2025 for the first time since 2021. Sequencing beyond the N-450 target has also increased since 2022, potentially improving transmission tracking. Among named strains, which represent frequently reported N-450 sequences, MVs/Gir Somnath.IND/42.16[D8] had the highest cumulative case count, with 6,595 recorded cases across 72 countries over a five-year period beginning in 2016. Rubella surveillance reveals major data gaps RuV molecular surveillance remains considerably more limited, with approximately one-tenth as many sequence submissions as measles. A shorter detection window, fewer detected cases, fewer accredited sequencing laboratories, lower viral RNA concentrations in clinical specimens, and the viral genome's high guanine-cytosine content may explain this gap. Rubella trends also varied by region. Reported cases in the AFR rose more than 20-fold, from 865 in 2000 to 19,669 in 2025, amid outbreaks in Nigeria, South Africa, and Uganda. The WPR peaked at 126,827 cases in 2008, before declining during 2020–2025. Some historical increases in reported cases may partly reflect improved surveillance sensitivity. Meanwhile, cases in the EUR and AMR fell approximately 1,000-fold since 2000. During the decade through 2025, approximately 247,000 rubella cases were reported globally, compared with more than 3.5 million measles cases. Incomplete reporting also means that the true rubella burden is likely higher. Fewer than one in 1,000 reported rubella cases were sequenced in previous years. Only 59 RuV sequences belonging to genotypes 1G and 2B were documented from 2022 onward, including just six in 2025. Genotype 2B has been the only genotype reported globally since 2024, while 1G, previously predominant in the AFR, was last reported in 2023. Genotype 1E predominated in the WPR during expanded surveillance between 2018 and 2020 but has not been reported since 2021. Limited sequencing coverage prevents definitive conclusions about whether other rubella genotypes have disappeared. Improving genomic surveillance and vaccination coverage “Sequence data alone cannot reliably reconstruct transmission patterns, particularly for measles.” Sustaining MR elimination will require investment in laboratory capacity, standardized sequencing protocols, quality assurance, surveillance, and vaccination. Whole-genome sequencing ( WGS ) and other extended sequencing approaches could improve the resolution of measles transmission tracking beyond the commonly used N-450 region. Their wider use is limited by costs, technical expertise, and inconsistent sequencing quality. Complete coding sequence ( CDS ) analysis could offer useful genetic detail while avoiding some technical challenges associated with non-coding regions, but its practical implementation would require high-throughput sequencing technology. Mutations identified through extended sequencing require interpretation alongside epidemiological data, case timing, and rates of genetic change in the virus, since longer genomic regions are naturally expected to contain more mutations. Named strains do not necessarily represent individual transmission chains. Differences in surveillance sensitivity, laboratory capacity, reporting completeness, and the proportion of laboratory-confirmed cases limit direct regional comparisons. Molecular surveillance must complement epidemiological investigations, with closer collaboration between laboratory scientists and epidemiologists needed to guide immunization efforts. No measles vaccine-escape strains have been reported. Maintaining high vaccination coverage and sensitive case detection remains central to MR elimination. Source: Journal reference: Weston, T., Cheng, C., Warrener, L. et al. (2026). Global Update on Measles and Rubella Molecular Epidemiology: 2000–2025. Vaccines , 14(11), 964. content_title: Measles outbreaks raise serious health concerns for expectant mothers and newborns
content: As measles infections increasingly appear in U.S. adults-a new CDC report is raising concerns about a heightened risk of congenital measles and infections in pregnant women. For expectant mothers, evidence suggests that infections can increase the risk of non-labor related hospitalizations, pneumonia, and death. Congenital measles can occur when a pregnant woman becomes infected with measles during pregnancy and passes the virus to the fetus in the womb. Infants can face severe illness, encephalitis, and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis-a rare, progressive, and often fatal neurological disorder. The new report, published in the New England Journal of Medicine Evidence, connects large measles outbreaks across the U.S. in 2025 and 2026 to 112 cases of measles in pregnant women and 13 cases of congenital measles in babies. In a November 25 episode of Public Health On Call, William Moss, MD, MPH, professor in Epidemiology, unpacks the new government analysis, including the measles threat to expectant mothers and newborns, and what it means in the context of ongoing outbreaks and the country's lapsed measles elimination status. Topics discussed: - The status of measles in the U.S., including current outbreaks in Pennsylvania and the nation's recent loss of elimination status - The new report from the CDC on congenital measles and why increases in adult measles infections are creating more openings for congenital measles - The possible health risks facing pregnant women who are infected with measles, and their newborns - How clinicians should approach measles vaccination and treatment for women of child-bearing age, pregnant women, and babies - The federal response to measles and congenital measles since 2025 Key quotes from the episode On the current status of measles and congenital measles in the U.S.: "Tragically we now have over 6,000 measles cases reported in the United States just this year." (01:54) "Earlier this month, on November 17, the Pan American Health Organization announced that the United States had lost its measles elimination status. Measles elimination is defined as no continuous transmission of the same measles virus strain for at least 12 months." (02:30) "A report from the Center for Disease Control and Prevention published in the New England Journal of Medicine Evidence ... report[ed] an astonishing 112 cases of measles in pregnant women and 13 cases of congenital measles." (03:10) "This is the largest case series that I'm aware of, of both measles in pregnancy and of congenital measles." (03:44) "According to the Center for Disease Control and Prevention, about 41% of measles cases in the United States have been in adults. If we look at Pennsylvania, for example, more than two-thirds of measles cases have been in adults 18 years or older." (04:02) "We're really seeing somewhat unusual demographic characteristics of the measles cases here in the United States, concentrated-or at least ... with high proportion-in adults." (04:18) On the health risks facing pregnant women who contract measles and their fetuses: "In the CDC report, almost a quarter of the women required hospitalization for non-labor related causes. Eleven of the 112, so about 10% of women, developed pneumonia. ... they're also at risk for serious birth outcomes: there can be stillbirths or miscarriages, premature births." (06:22) "During the last really big outbreak of measles here in the United States between 1989 and 1991 ... Pregnant women [with measles infections] were twice as likely to be admitted to the hospital, three times more likely to be diagnosed with pneumonia, and six times more likely to die of measles." (07:19) "We do know that infants ... with congenital measles can have some of the similar signs and symptoms of measles that we see in older children and adults: fever, rash." (8:10) "[Newborns are] also at risk for encephalitis, and there's even some suggestion ... that these infants may be at greater risk for a rare neurologic outcome called subacute sclerosing panencephalitis ... It's a severe, fatally progressive neurologic disease with a kind of defective measles virus in the brain." (08:27) On measles vaccination and treatment for pregnant women and infants: "Before pregnancy, make sure that you are vaccinated so that you are protected and can protect your infant." (15:37) "The measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine is not indicated during pregnancy, and that's in part because of that immune-suppressed state of pregnant women and the fact that these are attenuated viral vaccines, so they need to replicate in order to induce an immune response. So, we can't vaccinate women during pregnancy." (09:54) "Instead of what we call active immunization-giving a vaccine and inducing that person's immune system to be trained to fight that pathogen-we give what's called passive immunization. And so, it's something called intravenous immunoglobulin." (10:30) "Immunoglobulin is also recommended at birth for newborns who have been exposed to measles virus in utero, if the mom has measles late in the third trimester or prior to birth, and that too can reduce the morbidity associated with congenital measles." (11:10) "During pregnancy, what women need to do is really ensure that the people around them, their family members, their friends who they're coming into contact with, are vaccinated against measles to really reduce their risk of exposure." (16:01) On the response to measles from federal health officials: "We've not seen the strong response from the federal government that is needed promoting measles vaccination, and, in fact, we've seen the opposite." (14:30) "We've seen messaging that undermines public confidence in vaccines in general and the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine, specifically." (14:40) "I am sure that [the response from federal officials] has ... played a role in our loss of measles elimination status here in the United States and these continued large outbreaks. It's not the only explanation ... but the federal response has not helped and almost certainly set us back." (14:49)

content: Nearly 6 in 10 Americans hold government leaders responsible for the loss of the United States' measles elimination status, according to a new Ipsos poll. But there are few signs that the public wants to dwell on it. Why it matters: Partisan divisions over vaccines and outbreaks are so entrenched that Democrats won't have a broad mandate beyond their base to investigate the government's response when they take control of Congress. - There's also a generational divide. People age 65 and over — who remember the introduction of the measles vaccine — are more likely to say the current situation bothers them a lot. What they found: Roughly 3 in 5 Americans (58%) think the loss of the measles elimination status could have been prevented if government leaders had done a better job encouraging people to get vaccinated and responding to outbreaks. - 38% said there wasn't much government leaders could have done, because people make their own health decisions. - There's a huge partisan split behind those numbers: 84% of Democrats say the return of measles could have been avoided if the government had done a better job, compared with 38% of Republicans. Just over a quarter of Americans (26%) say they're extremely or very concerned about an outbreak occurring in their community. - There's a nearly 30-percentage-point partisan gap on concern, with 42% of Democrats extremely or very concerned, compared with 13% of Republicans. Independents are in the middle (25%). The findings come as Americans are sharply divided over the prospect of the next Congress investigating the Trump administration. And if COVID-19 is any guide, the public tends to be eager to put public health calamities in the rearview. - A Reuters-Ipsos post-election poll found that just 10% of Republicans said they want the new Congress to focus a great deal or quite a bit on investigating the Trump administration, compared with 71% of Democrats. - "As frustrating as the loss of measles elimination status is for many Americans, there's little in the [new] survey to suggest it will lead people who were not already supportive of investigating the administration to prioritize congressional oversight on this issue," said Alec Tyson, senior vice president of Ipsos U.S. Public Affairs. That isn't discouraging some Democrats on Capitol Hill. Incoming Senate health committee Chair Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said last week that Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s stewardship of the federal health apparatus during the measles outbreaks is "certainly one area that needs investigation." - House Energy and Commerce Democrats want to know whether the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention suppressed the number of measles deaths reported to the public. - They've also criticized agency director Erica Schwartz for not providing meaningful answers about decision-making around the reporting and response. The CDC has said it's committed to stopping outbreaks and regaining the measles elimination status. - It has pointed to actions like providing about $100 million in extra funding to strengthen prevention and response to measles and other vaccine-preventable diseases. What we're watching: Support for childhood vaccinations appears stronger than in the immediate aftermath of the pandemic. - Gallup this week found that more than 7 in 10 say it is extremely or very important for parents to get their children vaccinated — with the share saying it is extremely important 7 percentage points higher than in 2024. Methodology: The Ipsos poll was conducted Nov. 20-23, 2026, by Ipsos' KnowledgePanel®. This poll is based on a nationally representative probability sample of 1,022 general population adults age 18 or older. - The margin of sampling error is +/-3.2 percentage points at the 95% confidence level, for results based on the entire sample of adults

content: Health and Healthcare Systems US loses its status as measles-free, and other health stories Published Nov 24, 2026 A measles sign in New York.Image: REUTERS/Shannon Stapleton/File Photo After 26 years, the US can no longer claim to be free of measles following the continuing spread of the virus, while WHO and UNICEF are joining forces to tackle the global obesity issue. Read about these stories and more in this month’s round-up of top health news from around the world. 1. US declared no longer measles-free In a not-unexpected blow to the US, the country has lost its long-standing status of being free from the measles virus. Bolivia and Mexico have also lost their measles elimination status, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) announced on 17 November. The ruling “formalizes what was already plainly visible. The US has lost the ability to control measles," Dr Amesh Adalja, ​an infectious disease expert at the Johns Hopkins University Center for Health Security, told Reuters. Measles cases in the US have been on the increase in the past few years, with more than 2,200 cases recorded in 2025 and over 5,400 registered so far this year. This is compared to 59 cases in 2023 and 285 in 2024. Over 90% of the cases involve people who are unvaccinated, or their vaccination status is unknown, reports Science News. The affected countries will now need to prove that no one has caught measles within their borders for a full year in order to regain their measles-free status. To do so will require a huge turnaround in vaccination numbers, with 95% coverage required for herd immunity – as the chart above shows, coverage stood at 75% across the Americas in 2023. In response, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it had invested $100 million in vaccination programmes. Measles is on the rise once again. Here's how to fight it 01:42 2. WHO and UNICEF join forces to tackle global obesity issue More than 20 countries, led by Spain, have committed to a 5% reduction in national obesity rates by 2030, in a global call to action launched jointly by the World Health Organization (WHO) and UNICEF. This amounts to five fewer obese people in every 100, says WHO and UNICEF, while pointing out that “halting the rise is the first milestone” in countries with the highest obesity rates. In 2024, one in seven people – or 1.1 billion – were living with obesity, which in an adult constitutes a BMI of at least 30. More than a third of adults across the Americas are obese and 170 million children globally are living with obesity. Indeed, “there are now more school-age children with obesity than children who are underweight,” pointed out WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus at the launch of the project. “If obesity were a virus, it would be called a pandemic, and the world would be racing to stop it.” Worldwide adult obesity has more than doubled since 1990.Image: Our World in Data With obesity thought to be behind 3.7 million deaths a year – by contributing to cardiovascular diseases, diabetes and cancers – tackling the issue is both a health and economic imperative. The joint obesity strategy calls on governments to prioritize obesity as a chronic disease, and align financial and policy support accordingly. “The costs of obesity are counted in years of life lost, in strained health systems, and in the children and adolescents whose futures are derailed by chronic disease and lasting complications,” said the joint report. Read more on this topic Health and Healthcare Systems Healthier for longer: Taking care of our ageing societies by addressing obesity 3. News in brief: Health stories from around the world Ebola outbreak still not under control: Six months after it was first declared, the Ebola outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo remains out of control, reports Reuters, with both cases of the disease and deaths as a result of it continuing to rise. Over 11,000 people have been infected and over 5,500 ⁠have died since the outbreak began in May, which is double the rate seen in the first six months of the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak. El Niño a threat to pregnant women: Midwives have warned that millions of women in countries rated high risk for El Niño are in danger of dying during childbirth because they won’t have access to hospitals or healthcare. About 15 million babies are due to be born during the peak El Niño period, representing two-thirds of births worldwide, reports the Guardian. Alzheimer’s breakthroughs: Two drug trials have shown some success in treating Alzheimer’s. One trial involved a medicine usually used to treat schizophrenia that helped alleviate the symptoms of psychosis experienced by some Alzheimer’s patients. While a drug which targets the toxic tau protein in the brain was shown to slow cognitive decline in early Alzheimer’s patients by 38% after two years, reports Reuters. Hormone-disrupting chemicals found pre-birth: Babies can be exposed to endocrine-disrupting chemicals before birth, which can have lasting effects on brain development and growth, according to a new report from the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) and WHO. Exposure to these chemicals comes via everyday products and companies must work harder to “test early, disclose what is in their products, and get substitution right,” UNEP says. Eritrea eliminates trachoma: WHO has confirmed that Eritrea is the 11th African country and 34th globally to successfully eliminate trachoma – the leading infectious cause of blindness – as a public health problem. Globally, over 90 million people are still at risk of trachoma blindness. The news comes as the WHO presented its mid-term evaluation of its roadmap to eliminate neglected tropical diseases. Trachoma elimination stood at 65% in 2025 and the aim is for full elimination by 2030. Tuberculosis status update: WHO’s latest tuberculosis report finds that the global burden of TB is declining, with around 10.6 million people contracting the disease in 2025, a slight decrease on the previous year. That said, it’s still the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent and 2030 targets “remain distant”. 4. More on health from Forum Stories It’s estimated that around 80% of the world’s over-60s will be living in lower- and middle-income countries by 2030, with large numbers of these people in rural, underserved and impoverished areas. A coordinated effort is required to tackle this acute challenge, says Prakash Tyagi of GRAVIS. From pooling resources to transferring knowledge, this article gives a roadmap for government and societal response. Non-communicable diseases (NCD) cause three-quarters of deaths worldwide and 80% of those deaths are caused by just five conditions: heart disease, cancer, respiratory diseases, diabetes and kidney diseases. The following video explains the five key risk factors for developing an NCD – and the best prevention methods. These 5 health conditions cause the most deaths 01:58 The chronic underfunding of nurses is undermining a profession a conflicted world cannot do without, says the head of the International Council of Nurses. In this article, José Luis Cobos Serrano argues that the largest health workforce in the world needs to be better valued, empowered and backed by proper investment. “The strength of our health systems, our economies and our societies will depend largely on the decisions we make today regarding nursing,” he says. TBS Report 27 November, 2026, 04:05 pm Last modified: 27 November, 2026, 04:09 pm A mother carries her child suspected of having measles-like symptoms at a hospital in Bangladesh. File photo: UNB Seven more children died from measles and measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours until 8am today (27 November), taking the combined number of suspected and laboratory-confirmed measles-related deaths in Bangladesh to 1,378. Of the total deaths, 1,272 were suspected measles-related deaths, while 106 were confirmed through laboratory tests, according to the daily update of the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS). A total of 1,273 new suspected measles cases were reported during the 24-hour period, taking the cumulative number of suspected cases nationwide to 2,62,808. Keep updated, follow The Business Standard's Google news channel Meanwhile, 78 new laboratory-confirmed cases were recorded, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to 26,554. Since 15 March, a total of 2,35,482 patients with suspected measles have been hospitalised across the country. Of them, 2,26,440 have recovered, according to DGHS data. Set us as preferred To the editor: I took care of scores, if not hundreds, of children suffering from complications of measles, including pneumonia and encephalitis, over a period of three years as a pediatric house staff at a tertiary care center in India in the 1990s. Many of them died. I also saw subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, which is a less common but more lethal complication of measles. More recently, I was involved in an effort aimed at the education of U.S. physicians apropos neurological complications of vaccine-preventable diseases. The medical community in the U.S. is being prepared to handle the resurgence of diseases that many doctors here have never seen (“U.S. loses measles elimination status after first eradicating the disease 26 years ago,” Nov. 17). I am certain that they are going to be ready with the necessary knowledge. I am also certain that few are ready to handle the scars that come with taking care of children with devastating complications of easily preventable diseases. Jay Desai, Los Angeles This writer is a clinical professor at the University of Southern California and a neurologist at Children’s Hospital of Los Angeles.
